notes:
I've written notes for most verses of Proverbs 21, but not all. I ran out of search and fetch requests partway through. That left v. 22 thin and nothing at all for vv. 23–26 and 28.

**What I could and couldn't read**
- **Read in full:** the Pulpit Commentary page on StudyLight, but only up to v. 21, where it cut off.
- **Not readable:** Enduring Word was blocked. The Guzik page on Blue Letter Bible only loaded its menus, so I have his comments on vv. 1 and 30 from search previews only.
- **Mostly from search previews:** commentary pages on Bible Hub and StudyLight (Gill, Ellicott, Henry, Keil & Delitzsch, Clarke, NET notes and others).
- **Not reached at all:** the denominational sites (Ligonier aside), Bible Odyssey, and the Catholic and Orthodox sites. I found nothing on prosperity or word-of-faith readings.
- **Points without citation tags:** Pulpit notes taken from the full page carry a URL but no citation tags, because that page came through without sentence numbers.

---

**v. 1**
- Traditional reading: the picture is irrigation. The gardener controls the water completely and cuts channels wherever he likes. So God steers the king's heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-1.htm
- Kings are named not to leave other people out, but because kings are the least controllable of all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-1.htm
- Ligonier (Reformed): Kings and other national leaders can accomplish only what the Lord wills for them to accomplish. Because water gives life, it also sees the stress falling on God turning kings' hearts to bless His people. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-over-hearts-men
- Keil & Delitzsch balance this with human freedom. Man really is free, but acts under circumstances God directs, and God makes even rebellion serve His plan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-1.htm
- Guzik: God need not force the heart. He can arrange circumstances like banks of a river to guide where it flows. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-21.cfm
- Gill applies the verse to conversion too: God can turn anyone's understanding, will and affections as He pleases. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/proverbs/21-1.html
- A Bible Hub Q&A on wicked rulers separates God's "permissive" will from His "directive" will. God may let evil run while setting its limits. https://biblehub.com/q/how_can_god_direct_cruel_rulers'_hearts.htm

**v. 2**
- Pulpit links this to 16:2. It is a warning against self-deception and the smug belief that our own ways are best. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: Proverbs often teaches that moral obedience outranks ceremony (it cites Micah 6:6–8 and Matthew 12:7). It says "justice and judgment" flow from love, not bare legal duty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html
- Chuck Smith ties it to Jesus rebuking those who tithed spices "You've totally omitted the more important things: righteousness, mercy, judgment." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/21-12.html

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: "haughty eyes" means looking down on others, and the proud heart causes the proud look.
- A text question: one Hebrew pointing gives "ploughing/tillage" (KJV), meaning everything the wicked cultivate is sin. Another gives "lamp" (Vulgate, Septuagint), meaning the wicked's prosperity, built on self, is itself sinful. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: patient work is rewarded. The "haste" here is the rush to get rich by any means, even crooked ones, and it ends in want. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: wealth gained by lies is as fleeting as a breath and ends in death. Some see a desert mirage in the image. The Septuagint and Vulgate read "snares of death," and Pulpit links this to 1 Timothy 6:9. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: the violence the wicked do to others comes back on them. That is fitting punishment for deliberately refusing to do right. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: the KJV's "and strange" is really one Hebrew word meaning "laden with guilt," giving "crooked is the way of a guilty man." The pure in heart act rightly and go straight ahead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: the flat roof was a usable room, but a cramped corner of it is still better than sharing a house with a quarrelsome woman. That may be a wife or another female relative. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html
- Matthew Henry (Concise): It is best to shun bitter contention by pouring out the heart before God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-18.htm

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: the wicked man can't rest without planning new evil and will sacrifice even those close to him. The Septuagint reads it passively: no one will pity him, which Pulpit links to "Blessed are the merciful." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: the simple learn from the mocker's punishment, while the wise learn without needing it. It quotes St Gregory: seeing truth's despisers flourish unsettles the weak, but just punishment keeps them from sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 12 (the verse where readings differ most)**
- Pulpit and Keil & Delitzsch: "a Righteous One" is God. Pulpit says the subject doesn't change between the two lines. "a righteous One" (tsaddik) is God, put indeterminately to excite the greater awe https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html
- Barnes (labelled Presbyterian) also reads it as Yahweh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-12.htm
- Ellicott: God watches to see whether the wicked will repent, and overthrows them when their wickedness is full. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/21-12.htm
- Matthew Henry (labelled Nonconformist/Calvinist) keeps "righteous man." A godly person who looks with faith sees the curse on the wicked's house and stops envying it. He also mentions a reading where a magistrate searches the house. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/21-12.html
- Adam Clarke (labelled Wesleyan/Methodist) reads it as a righteous man's caring concern for a wicked family, whom he tries to teach the way of peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/21-12.html
- Catholic tradition: the Douay-Rheims follows the Vulgate, "that he may withdraw the wicked from evil." https://biblehub.com/proverbs/21-12.htm Pulpit calls that idea "quite foreign" to the verse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html
- A caution: these are individual commentators. I found no source saying whole denominations divide here.

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: the unmerciful man will cry for help in vain, including at the final judgment (it cites Luke 6:38 and James 2:13). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html
- Henry includes those who hold down wages, won't help as they can, or neglect justice when in power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-14.htm

**v. 14**
- Most commentators read it as an observation, not approval. Bible Hub: The point is descriptive, not permissive. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/21-14.htm
- Coffman agrees: bribery works, but God doesn't approve it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/21-14.html
- Henry: a well-handled gift can calm anger (Jacob and Esau, Abigail and David). But a bribe that perverts justice is shameful even to those who like it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/21-14.html
- Henry's Concise asks: if money can tame passion, can't reason and the fear of God do it? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-14.htm
- Gill notes some Jewish readers took it as alms that calm God's anger, written on the poor box, though he prefers the plain sense. The Septuagint and Syriac reverse it: holding back gifts stirs wrath. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: the righteous find real joy in doing right. The second line means doing right is a "terror" to evildoers, who can't trust God with the outcome. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: "the dead" is *rephaim*. The verse threatens early death, and Pulpit sees a hint of punishment after death. The Church Fathers took the rephaim as giants descended from the fallen angels, and St Gregory linked them to the proud spirits. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html
- Henry's Concise: there is hope even for these wanderers in Christ, if they flee to Him without delay. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-18.htm

**v. 17**
- Pulpit: wine and oil were the trappings of a banquet. Costly ointments point to extravagance, which leads to ruin, and spiritual poverty too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 18**
- Traditional reading: the wicked fall into the trouble meant for the righteous. Examples given are Haman and Mordecai, and Achan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-18.htm
- Gill stresses this is not a ransom in the sense of making satisfaction, as Christ is for His people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-18.htm
- Bible Hub's study notes do see a picture of Christ, the sinless ransom. https://biblehub.com/study/proverbs/21-18.htm But a Pulpit homily warns not to blur the plain meaning: in disaster, the faithful escape. https://biblehub.com/sermons/proverbs/21-18.htm
- Modern scholarship (NET notes, citing Whybray): if the verse meant the wicked get good things meant for the righteous, it would be a despairing cry, which is unusual for Proverbs. Reading it as the wicked suffering what they planned fits the rest of the book. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=pro&chapter=21&verse=18
- Clarke: God often cuts off the wicked to stop them destroying the righteous. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/21-18.html

**v. 19**
- Pulpit: this is a variant of v. 9. Many read it as "a quarrelsome wife and the vexation" she brings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html
- Henry's Concise: uncontrolled passions spoil every relationship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-12.htm

**v. 20**
- Pulpit: the wise store up provisions to be generous and to prepare for the future, while the fool swallows them up. Spiritually, the wise store grace and the fool squanders it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 21**
- Pulpit: "mercy" is *chesed*, love shown to others. The second "righteousness" is God's gift of grace to live a holy life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html
- Henry's Concise: true repentance and faith lead the person who trusts God's mercy in Christ to pursue righteousness and mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-12.htm

**v. 22**
- Henry's Concise: in spiritual warfare we put on God's armour, but our strength must be in the Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/21-12.htm

**v. 27**
- Smith: God doesn't really want sacrifices from the wicked. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/21-12.html

**v. 29**
- Pulpit: modern commentators prefer the marginal Hebrew reading, "he considers" his way. The upright man acts only after careful thought. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-21.html

**v. 30**
- Guzik: To fight against God is to fight a losing battle. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-21.cfm

**v. 31**
- Coffman, quoting the Tyndale commentary: v. 30 warns against fighting God, and v. 31 against fighting without Him. Resources are allowed, but relying on them is condemned. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/21-31.html
- Henry: means must still be used, and the horse prepared. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/21-31.html
- Ellicott and Clarke note that Solomon's horses from Egypt broke Deuteronomy 17:16. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/21-31.htm https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/proverbs/21-31.html
- Pulpit applies it spiritually: our only safety against spiritual enemies is God's grace (1 Corinthians 15:57). https://biblehub.com/proverbs/21-31.htm
